qs.q: A patient with a rare genetic defect exhibits fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly due to glycogen storage disease type VI (Hers disease). Why does liver glycogen accumulation occur in this condition?
o: Defected debranching enzyme prevents outer chain removal
Mutated glycogen synthase remains constitutively active without insulin
Impaired hepatic phosphorylase prevents breakdown to glucose-1-phosphate
Absence of glucose-6-phosphatase traps glucose inside the hepatocytes
Deficiency of branching enzyme creates abnormal insoluble polymers
qs.e: Hers disease involves liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, blocking the initial cleavage of glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate.

qs.q: A patient with suspected glycogen storage disease undergoes a forearm ischemic exercise test, showing markedly blunted lactate production in venous blood alongside normal muscle phosphorylase activity. Which alternative enzymatic defect is most consistent?
o: Deficiency of hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme activity
Deficiency of lysosomal alpha-glucosidase enzyme activity
Deficiency of muscle carnitine palmitoyltransferase enzyme
Deficiency of muscle phosphofructokinase-1 enzyme activity
Deficiency of hepatocyte glycogen phosphorylase enzyme
qs.e: Phosphofructokinase-1 deficiency in muscle impairs glycolysis early, preventing normal lactate accumulation during ischemic exercise.

qs.q: Von Gierke's disease (Type 1 glycogen storage disease) is caused by
o: Acid maltase (alpha-glucosidase) deficiency → glycogen in lysosomes
Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency → glycogen and fat accumulation in liver and kidneys
Debranching enzyme deficiency → limit dextrin accumulation
qs.e: Von Gierke (GSD Type 1): G6Pase deficiency → glucose cannot be released from liver → severe fasting hypoglycemia + massive hepatomegaly + renomegaly + hyperlipidemia + hyperuricemia (gout). Lactic acidosis. Treatment: continuous glucose/cornstarch feeds.

qs.q: Pompe's disease (GSD Type 2) is caused by acid maltase deficiency and is unique among glycogen storage diseases because
o: Glycogen accumulates in lysosomes (a lysosomal storage disease)
qs.e: Pompe = only GSD that is also a lysosomal storage disease. Glycogen accumulates in lysosomes of heart, skeletal muscle, liver. Infantile form: cardiomegaly, hypotonia, respiratory failure → death by age 2. Treatment: enzyme replacement (alglucosidase alfa). Remember: "Pompe trashes the pump" (heart).

ai.title: Glycogen Storage Diseases
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Inherited enzyme defects that disturb glycogen synthesis or breakdown, leading to hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly and organ‑specific damage. Clinical reasoning focuses on history, bedside clues and pragmatic investigations in low‑resource settings.

b: Most common in East Africa: GSD‑I (glucose‑6‑phosphatase deficiency) and GSD‑III (debranching enzyme deficiency).
sections.p: Glycogen storage diseases (GSDs) are autosomal recessive defects in enzymes that control glycogen metabolism. They present in infancy or early childhood with hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, growth failure and organ‑specific signs.

b: Glucose‑6‑phosphatase (GSD‑I) – blocks final step of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Debranching enzyme (GSD‑III) – impairs removal of branch points, leading to abnormal glycogen.
sections.p: Normal glycogen synthesis stores glucose; glycogenolysis releases glucose during fasting. Enzyme defects block either synthesis or breakdown, causing accumulation or depletion of glucose.

b: In GSD‑I, fasting hypoglycaemia is severe because glucose‑6‑phosphatase is absent; in GSD‑III, hypoglycaemia is milder but muscle cramps occur.
sections.p: Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis; glucagon and epinephrine stimulate glycogenolysis. In GSDs, these hormonal signals cannot overcome the enzymatic block.

b: GSD‑I – severe fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, hyperlipidaemia, hepatomegaly, renal tubular dysfunction.
GSD‑III – hepatomegaly, mild hypoglycaemia, myopathy, cardiomyopathy, fatty liver.
sections.p: The defect determines the clinical picture:
In low‑resource hospitals, patients present with recurrent hypoglycaemia, vomiting, lethargy, hepatomegaly and growth faltering. Early recognition prevents liver failure and death.

Hepatic glycogenosis in malaria or viral hepatitis – hepatomegaly but normal glucose metabolism.
sections.p: Other causes of hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly can mimic GSDs.

t.a: What is the most common GSD in East Africa?
t.b: GSD‑I (glucose‑6‑phosphatase deficiency) is most frequently encountered.
Yes, dilated cardiomyopathy can develop, especially in adolescence.

t.a: Is there a cure for GSDs?
t.b: No definitive cure; management focuses on dietary control and monitoring for complications.

t.a: A 10‑month‑old boy presents with recurrent vomiting, lethargy after 6 hours of fasting, and a firm hepatomegaly. Blood g
t.b: Glycogen storage disease type I (glucose‑6‑phosphatase deficiency).

t.a: What is the first step in managing this patient?
t.b: Start continuous feeding with high‑carbohydrate feeds or uncooked cornstarch every 4–6 hours.

t.a: Which laboratory finding would help distinguish GSD‑I from ketotic hypoglycaemia?
t.b: Absence of ketones in the urine in GSD‑I.

t.a: A child with GSD‑III develops muscle cramps and cardiomyopathy. Which investigation is most useful?
t.b: Echocardiogram to assess ventricular function.

t.a: Why is allopurinol avoided in a patient with renal tubular dysfunction?
t.b: It can worsen renal impairment and cause uric acid nephropathy.

t.a: What is the key clinical sign that suggests hepatic glycogenosis due to malaria rather than a GSD?
t.b: Presence of fever, splenomegaly, and positive malaria smear.

t.a: Which dietary component should be limited in GSD‑I to prevent gout?
t.b: Purine‑rich foods that increase uric acid production.
